decisions.title: The journey definition establishes the channel, for every channel
decisions.reasoning:
Channel was derived from the session's device class, which works only for interactive sessions — and the model states that api and agent callers have no device. So the two non-interactive channels had no stated source at all, which is a hole in a Level-1 dimension rather than a modelling nicety.

The answer was already in the model, unused. Journey definitions carry servesChannel, and every session is established by an execution that follows a definition, so the chain from session to channel was complete but never relied upon. It works uniformly: a client-credentials definition serves api, a passkey definition serves web, and the derivation never asks whether a device exists.

It is also the better provenance. Journey definitions are governed desired state flowing through the declaration machinery, so the channel now derives from an approved artifact rather than from configuration nobody signed. followsDefinition is consequently mandatory: an execution with no definition is an ungoverned authentication path and a session whose channel cannot be established, which was previously only a warning.

The device class is demoted to corroboration. Each class declares the channel it implies, and a session whose device contradicts its journey's channel is a violation — misconfiguration, or a mobile client presenting as a browser.
rejected: Deriving channel from the route: a single application is commonly reachable on both web and api, and routes are per-application, so this would force routes to multiply per channel for a fact the journey already holds.
An explicit channel property on the session: simplest, but it relocates the question rather than answering it, and creates a second place that can disagree with the journey.
decisions.$caveat: Assumes every api and agent caller authenticates through something modelled as a journey, including one-event client-credentials executions. A caller presenting credentials directly to ingress, bypassing the session manager, would have no journey and no derivable channel.

decisions.title: A device is nameable, and its class describes the client not the hardware
decisions.reasoning:
Device carried exactly one property — its class — so a PDP context that names a requesting client could say the category was Browser but never which client. A concurrency limit counts sessions per device, and an unnamed device cannot be counted, so identity was load-bearing rather than cosmetic. Device now requires a canonical identifier, and core:identifier was generalised from an enumeration of principal kinds to any entity's registry identifier.

The class definition was also wrong in a way worth correcting rather than living with. Its members are Browser and Mobile, which are client software types, not hardware and not operating systems — the same axis Microsoft calls 'client apps' and keeps separate from device platforms and from a specific registered device. The definition now says it classifies the requesting client.

The fuller correction — splitting client type from device the way Microsoft does — was deliberately not taken. It would churn the concurrency invariants, which are keyed to device class, and it is a vocabulary decision for the security architecture group rather than an inference.
rejected: Splitting client type from device entirely, per Microsoft's three-way division into client apps, device platforms and device filters: the right end state, but it churns invariants and is a decision to take with the review group.
Leaving Device unnameable: a concurrency limit that counts per device cannot count anonymous ones.

decisions.title: Decisions name the point that made them; XACML is the settled vocabulary
decisions.reasoning:
The platform and each application run their own policy decision point, but nothing recorded which one rendered a decision — PolicyDecisionPoint existed, was generic, and was never instantiated. Only the decision's class distinguished a platform decision from any other, so 'show me everything the platform PDP decided' was unanswerable and an application decision misfiled as a platform one would not have been caught.

decidedBy is now mandatory on every decision, and the seed instantiates the platform PDP alongside the enforcement point it already had — the XACML pair, both present.

On vocabulary: XACML is the settled source. Its four outcomes were already the scheme, and its request-context categories are now alt-labels on the tuple properties — subject on requestingPrincipal, action on evaluatedAction, resource on targetsResource — so a reader coming from XACML finds the platform's terms by searching its own. 'Allow' is an alt-label on Permit rather than a rename: the outcome vocabulary stays XACML, and the synonym is there for findability rather than as a second name.
rejected: A PlatformPolicyDecisionPoint subclass to separate the two PDPs by type: unnecessary while application decisions are out of scope and never enter the graph, and it would imply a symmetric ApplicationPolicyDecisionPoint that the Level-3 boundary forbids. Worth revisiting only if application decisions are ever ingested for audit.
Renaming the Permit outcome to Allow: the outcome scheme is XACML's, and renaming one member would leave the vocabulary half-aligned.

decisions.title: A route serving an application is the application access endpoint
decisions.reasoning:
The platform PDP's question — may this subject enter this application through this endpoint — could not be answered. Four of its five joins existed, but nothing linked a route to an application: routes reached an UpstreamService, and no UpstreamService named an Application.

Run as SPARQL the question returned zero rows. Drop the missing join and it returned a plausible row, which was worse: the only thing tying application to endpoint was that both belonged to the same tenant, so a tenant owning three applications would have matched all three at any of its routes. The model would have answered 'may enter' for an application the endpoint does not serve — a false positive, the direction that fails open.

One property closes it. servesApplication makes a tenant-bound route the addressable endpoint an application is entered at: it already carried the domain, the path, the tenant binding, the mediating enforcement point, and a governed declaration behind the binding. Route now carries 'application access endpoint' as an alt-label, so the architecture diagrams and the ontology use one vocabulary.

Two invariants follow — a route must not serve an application its bound tenant does not own, and must not serve one at a scope outside that application's enablement — and the question becomes CQ-7, executed by CI.
rejected: Linking UpstreamService to Application instead: an upstream is a backend the route forwards to, and several may serve one application; the endpoint is what a subject enters through.
Leaving the join implicit through shared tenant ownership: it returns rows, which is precisely why it is dangerous — the answer looks right and fails open.

decisions.title: Two clients, kept apart
decisions.reasoning:
The word 'client' names two unrelated things, and conflating them is how a platform ends up making entitlement decisions from a protocol identifier.

The OAuth client is the session manager's registration at the identity provider, one per audience. Its client_id identifies that registration and nothing else — no tenancy, no channel, no caller identity — and it is derivable from the audience. It is modelled as authn:OAuthClientRegistration, deliberately thin, and carries an editorial note that entitlement decisions must never be made from a client_id.

The business client is a party holding a relationship with the firm: the customer, retail or corporate. It is core:BusinessClient, and it is not itself authenticable — principals act for it. That separation is what lets one corporate client have many users, and lets one person hold both a staff identity and a client relationship without the model confusing them.

This also spends a reservation the model has held since the naming work on registrations: 'client' was kept free for the firm's business meaning rather than being used for software, and this is that meaning taking its place.
rejected: One Client class covering both: the two share a word and nothing else — one is protocol bookkeeping, the other is a business relationship with a lifecycle.
Making BusinessClient a subclass of Principal: a corporate client is not authenticable and has many users, so principals act for a client rather than being one.
Leaving the OAuth registration unmodelled as pure plumbing: it is plumbing, but naming it explicitly is what stops the two senses of 'client' collapsing back together in conversation.

decisions.title: One logical management control plane
decisions.reasoning: A single governance authority platform-wide; regional replicas are deployment topology, not model citizens. Blast radius is partitioned by scoped declarations, not by forking governance truth. Per-region planes would partition authority (drift-prone) where the actual need is partitioned blast radius. Choose per-region planes only if regulators force governance data itself to be region-confined.

decisions.title: Control planes are logical components
decisions.reasoning: One CapabilityControlPlane individual per capability; regional deployments appear as multiple acting identities rather than multiple control-plane individuals. Deployment topology belongs in a CMDB; the audit questions are about the logical writer.

decisions.title: Scope tree, mandatory on declarations
decisions.reasoning: A single-parent tree carries authority, locality containment and approval-rigor inheritance; environment/region facets on nodes carry cross-cutting dimensions. Single-parent by design: DAG inheritance is ambiguous the moment two parents disagree, and conflict-resolution rules for governance metadata are exactly the complexity auditors should not have to re-derive. Scope is mandatory because 'global' should be an explicit root-scope choice someone made, never a default you get by forgetting a triple.
rejected: Two orthogonal axis-properties (environment + region): clean for env×region, silent on tenants, and every future axis needs invariant surgery.
Flat named scopes: no inheritance or containment reasoning; all meaning trapped in naming conventions.

decisions.title: Locality
decisions.reasoning: A mutation's data plane must fall inside its declaration's scope, checked by containment through the scope tree. This is what makes scoped governance real rather than advisory, and it is the mechanism that delivers blast-radius containment without forking governance authority.

decisions.title: Declarations immutable and approved
decisions.reasoning: New intent means a new individual; a supersedes chain versions them. Realizing an unapproved declaration is a violation; realizing a superseded one is only a warning, because a reconciler catching up to yesterday's intent is operational reality, not a breach. Immutability is what makes the audit chain meaningful: if declarations could be silently rewritten, the provenance chain would prove nothing.

decisions.title: Scope-dependent approval rigor
decisions.reasoning: Scopes carry the approval requirement, inherited to the nearest ancestor that says anything: prod strict, dev light, one constraint, zero shape exceptions. Data-driven rigor keeps the invariant count constant and makes 'which scopes waive human approval' a governed, queryable fact — an auditor question you want answerable.

decisions.title: Sole writer, exactly one per data plane
decisions.reasoning: Mutations execute under the acting identity of the data plane's designated writer; the management plane never actuates a data plane (tier skipping); no capability control plane administers the scope holding its own declarations (self-governance loop). Governance is separated from actuation, and each half is machine-checked rather than assumed.

decisions.title: Data-driven isolation models
decisions.reasoning: Each capability declares its isolation model ('shared' or 'cell-per-tenant') and one constraint enforces whatever the capability claims, rather than a hand-written shape per capability. The invariant count stays constant as capabilities multiply, and the isolation model becomes a governed, queryable fact. The constraint this decision describes was not in the shapes until P16's promotion surfaced the gap; IsolationModelShape now exists and demonstrably fires (D54).

decisions.title: Tenant, Capability and Application promoted to core
decisions.reasoning: These are platform-wide primitives every module must see: ingress-layer work needs tenancy and applications, but ingress imports only core. Moved while all terms were draft and unconsumed — a free structural correction that would have been a MAJOR-version migration later.

decisions.title: The platform is a distinguished tenant
decisions.reasoning: PlatformTenant is a singleton subclass of Tenant, so ownership stays single-ranged with no or-branches anywhere, and the platform holds capability subscriptions like any tenant — keeping every coverage rule uniform. Modelled as a subclass rather than a boolean flag so tenant-level queries can include or exclude it by type, containing the risk that platform-owned assets silently sweep into tenant reporting.
rejected: A separate Platform class outside the Tenant hierarchy: ontologically honest (the platform does not onboard or offboard) but forces an or-ranged ownedBy and or-branches into every ownership shape and query.

decisions.title: Subscriptions: first-class, capability-only, scope-free
decisions.reasoning: A subscription is a first-class object with an access-relevant lifecycle (no billing states) and a validity window, because 'when did this tenant gain this, who approved it, is it still active' is exactly what auditors ask and a bare triple cannot answer. Subscriptions target capabilities only — applications are owned, not subscribed. They are scope-free: where a capability is usable is computed as subscription ∩ entitlement grants ∩ offerings, so each authority states one thing and none can contradict another.
rejected: Scoped subscriptions ('DBaaS in EU-prod'): creates a second place where region and environment live, permanently able to contradict the tenant's entitlement grants, which would then need a precedence rule — a design smell.

decisions.title: Subscription activation is always human-approved
decisions.reasoning: A tenant gaining a capability changes what it can reach — the meta-authorization boundary the control-plane module exists to guard. Uniform rule, platform tenant included: slightly ceremonial for the platform subscribing to itself, but one rule everywhere and system capabilities get the same audit trail.

decisions.title: Provisioning is justified by a subscription
decisions.reasoning: Tenant-provisioning declarations carry justifiedBy, completing a provenance chain rare in platform models: subscription → declaration → mutation → data plane, every hop human-approvable and machine-checkable. Teardown declarations reference the terminated subscription, so the invariant is about the subscription existing rather than being currently active — otherwise deprovisioning would violate it.

decisions.title: Hard dependencies only; closure; acyclic
decisions.reasoning: Dependencies are hard-only until a real soft case appears (YAGNI applies to edge types too); the closure is auto-included and materialized at subscription time so 'what does this tenant hold' stays a flat read; and the dependency graph must be a DAG, which SHACL checks in one line with a property path.

decisions.title: Bundles expand at subscription time
decisions.reasoning: A bundle is a named set — sales-time convenience. Subscribing expands it to per-capability subscriptions, so enforcement, reachability and every competency question only ever see capabilities. Treating bundles as products with their own identity would force bundle-awareness into every enforcement path and query forever.

decisions.title: Offerings: no cross-scope parity
decisions.reasoning: A capability exists where an offering says it does — parity across regions and environments cannot be assumed. Offerings are governed intent (so 'we launch in APAC next quarter' is representable before hardware exists) and data planes must conform: deployed-where-not-offered is a violation, because infrastructure existing outside governance is exactly what a bank wants caught; offered-but-undeployed is launch tracking. A supply-side closure forbids offering a capability where its hard dependencies are not covered.

decisions.title: Applications are owned, distinct from capabilities
decisions.reasoning: Exactly one owning tenant (possibly the platform tenant); transfer is declaration supersession, never co-ownership. Applications and capabilities stay distinct classes because one is owned and consumes while the other is subscribed and provides — and because collapsing them would invite exactly the vocabulary leak the ingress boundary principle forbids.

decisions.title: Requirements: observed, then human-confirmed
decisions.reasoning: 'Agents observe, humans confirm.' Windowed aggregate observations (never per-request) propose capability requirements; a human approval confirms them; only confirmed requirements gate enablement, and drift is watched in both directions. Pure declared manifests rot and lie; pure observation would mean an access model that learns its rules by watching violations happen, inverting intent-precedes-actuation. The hybrid makes observation the auditor rather than the gatekeeper.

decisions.title: The enablement gate
decisions.reasoning: Enablement is a declaration, so scope, approval rigor and supersession apply for free rather than needing a second mechanism. It is gated on the owner's active subscriptions covering the application's confirmed requirements AND on offerings covering the enablement scope — both halves, since no parity is assumed. This is the keystone invariant joining ownership, curation, subscription and closure.

decisions.title: Portals are presentation only
decisions.reasoning: Tenant-owned groupings of applications. Admission stays per-application and the enforcement vocabulary never learns the word 'portal'; disabling a portal is a governance macro over enablement declarations, not an enforcement concept. Coherence is enforced: grouped applications must belong to the portal's owner. Whether a portal is per delivery channel is left open — the channel of a request comes from the session's device class, not from anything a portal declares.

decisions.title: Five entitlement dimensions in a closed scheme
decisions.reasoning: platform / tenant / environment / region / channel, as a closed SKOS scheme owned by authz. The closure is the point: it makes 'deliberately small, stable, platform-owned' machine-checkable rather than aspirational, so no application team can introduce its own entitlement model into unified ingress. It lives in authz because that module already requires security-architecture review — precisely the gate you want on a vocabulary whose value is that it changes rarely and deliberately.
rejected: A subclass per dimension: no benefit over ranked individuals, and every new dimension becomes a class-hierarchy change.

Reusing AttributeAssertion: conflates an observation (the HR system reports a fact) with a conferral (someone granted access), and loses the closed-vocabulary check since attribute names are open strings by design.
client.access as a sixth dimension: the registration is the evidence for the channel dimension, not a dimension itself.

decisions.title: Grants are projections, never hand-authored
decisions.reasoning: An entitlement grant is the materialized projection of upstream governance — a subscription, a registration, an enablement — with derivation mandatory and a distribution timestamp anchoring staleness queries. The token is evidence; the grant is authority. This is what makes revocation take effect without re-minting tokens, and it is the continuous-access-evaluation philosophy CAEP exists to serve.

decisions.title: Channel is the capability delivery channel
decisions.reasoning: web, mobile, api, agent — the avenue through which platform capabilities are consumed, resolved from the session's device class rather than any self-asserted claim. M2M was dropped: east-west service traffic largely does not cross unified ingress, and workload identity already governs it. Agent-channel delegation semantics are deliberately deferred to backlog questions, since delegation modelled casually is worse than absent.

decisions.title: The ingress token contract
decisions.reasoning: Ingress assembles context from three sources, and the token is only one of them. The request host and path resolve the tenant; the ingress deployment that received the request resolves environment and region; the session cookie's opaque handle resolves the session. The token contributes identity and assurance: sub through a subject identifier to a principal, acr/amr/auth_time to the journey execution. None of these is an entitlement — a token asserting 'I am allowed in prod' would invert the evidence/authority split. Ingress deliberately ignores scope and permissions claims: those are Level-3, application-owned. Two of the three sources are currently unmodelled: domain and path are bound to a tenant in ingress route configuration, but the ingress module has no host or path matching and no tenant binding; and the cookie-to-session resolution has no representation at all. Both are recorded gaps rather than settled design.
rejected: Minting entitlements into the token: claims freeze at issuance, so an entitlement stays true until expiry — exactly the window in which offboarding or compromise must take effect.
Treating tenancy as a token claim: tenant context comes from the request URL in this platform, so a claim would duplicate it and the two could disagree.

decisions.title: The flagship reachability question
decisions.reasoning: For a token or principal-session pair: which resources are reachable, and through which chain? Reachable = grants ∩ enablement scopes ∩ subscriptions ∩ offerings ∩ token audience ∩ effective AAL. The explanation form — returning the chain rather than just the set — is what makes access reviews tractable, and the audience-minting invariant uses it as a subroutine.

decisions.title: Journeys in scope — definitions and executions
decisions.reasoning: User journeys enter the ontology narrowly, as authentication journeys — orchestrated flows by which a principal establishes or elevates authentication. Governed definitions per channel (whose changes flow through the declaration machinery) plus executions comprising the events actually traversed. Both halves are needed: without definitions you cannot ask what was configured; without executions you cannot ask what was completed; and only having both makes 'which sessions deviate from their definition' expressible.

decisions.title: Sessions re-bound to journey executions
decisions.reasoning: establishedBy was retargeted from a single AuthenticationEvent to a journey execution while every term was still draft — a free structural correction that would have become a MAJOR-version migration the week a consumer shipped. Achieved assurance moved to the execution because AAL is a property of completing the flow, not of any single step: password alone achieves nothing, password+OTP achieves AAL2. Single-step flows such as passkeys are simply one-event executions, so nothing gets more complicated for simple cases.

decisions.title: Step-up elevations; effective AAL is the latest successful
decisions.reasoning: A step-up is an elevation execution linked to the same session, not a new session. Effective AAL is the latest successful execution's — cheap in SPARQL and semantically honest if a re-authentication ever lands lower than an earlier elevation. Freshness decay is policy, not session structure: a policy demanding 'AAL3 within the last 10 minutes' compares the elevation's timestamp at decision time, which the model already supports. The shipped guard checks that some successful execution meets the requirement — identical while executions are monotonic, and flagged for revisiting when decay lands.

decisions.title: AuthorizedParty — reinstated, then removed as unfounded
decisions.reasoning:
Recorded as a reversal rather than deleted, because the reasoning failed in an instructive way. Standards review found that tokens carry a client identifier with no home in the model, and I inferred that it pointed at tenant-owned, channel-bound request-originating software — a portal's web front, a partner daemon. On that premise AuthorizedParty was introduced with an owning tenant, a channel binding, and an issuedTo edge from every token.

The premise was wrong. The OAuth client is the session manager, the platform maintains one client registration per audience, and client_id is only a protocol identifier: it carries no tenancy and no channel. Both defining properties of the class were therefore false, and what remained was derivable from the audience — putting it in the same category as JOSE header fields, which the model excludes as plumbing below the semantic layer.

Removed in full: the class, boundToChannel, session:issuedTo, cp:frontedBy, authn:scopedToParty and the shapes and tests that depended on them. The lesson worth keeping is that a gap identified from a standard rather than from the architecture is a hypothesis, and this one should have been checked before it was modelled.
rejected: Keeping a hollowed-out AuthorizedParty with the false properties stripped: what remained was an OAuth registration identifier derivable from the audience, adding nothing the model needs.
Retargeting it to the session manager's per-audience registration: that is real, but it is protocol bookkeeping with no competency question behind it.

decisions.title: Subject identifiers as first-class naming facts
decisions.reasoning: 'At issuer Y, subject X denotes principal P' had no home: core:identifier is the firm-canonical name, not the per-issuer and possibly pairwise subject that OIDC and RFC 9493 require. Reified with value, issuer, principal, format and an optional pairwise scope to an authorized party, plus a validity window because issuers recycle subjects (email especially). Read in reverse at resolution time: a token or CAEP event carries the subject, this node yields the principal. One (issuer, value) combination must never denote two principals — the account-takeover-by-collision check.
rejected: A multi-valued datatype property: stringly-typed, with no home for pairwise scoping, formats or validity, and uniqueness unenforceable without string surgery.
A Credential subclass: a subject identifier proves nothing and is presented by no one — it is a naming fact, not an authentication artifact.
AttributeAssertion reuse: assertions describe a known principal to feed decisions; identifiers resolve an unknown subject to a principal — opposite direction, different consumer.

decisions.title: Actions on decisions — the AuthZEN tuple completed
decisions.reasoning: Decisions recorded subject, resource and outcome but not the action attempted, leaving AuthZEN's evaluation tuple incomplete: every decision said who, where and what was answered, but not what was asked. Added as a closed, platform-owned SKOS scheme (access, read, write, administer, with AuthZEN wire names as notations) required exactly once on every decision. Two invariants: tuple completeness, and the Level-3 boundary enforced at the decision layer — application verbs like 'approve payment' must never reach platform decisions. The slot was originally called 'capability' in the architecture write-up; renamed to 'action' because capability now names platform offerings.
rejected: A datatype property with a string action name: free strings drift (read/READ/view) and the Level-3 boundary becomes unenforceable.
Reifying the whole request as an AccessRequest node: no competency question demands it, and PolicyDecision already is the reified evaluation record.

decisions.title: Admission decisions evaluate the platform admission policy
decisions.reasoning: The decision shape requires an evaluated policy, but admission evaluates distributed grants — so every admission decision had to either fake a policy reference or violate. Resolved by declaring the distributed entitlement configuration to BE a Policy instance ('the platform admission policy'), which is true by the model's own definition of Policy as a named, versioned unit of authorization logic. Keeps one shape and gives policy-change governance a hook on admission configuration. Admission decisions additionally require exactly one channel and at least one evaluated grant: admission without grants is admission without authority.

decisions.title: Resources act through principals
decisions.reasoning: Resources cannot be principals, so anything that acts needs a principal to act as. hasActingIdentity was promoted from control-plane to core for this, and control plane components use it so their writes are attributable under the sole-writer invariant. It was also applied to authorized parties for headless consumers; that half went away with the class, but the pattern and the promotion stand.

decisions.title: Portal coherence
decisions.reasoning: Nothing prevented a portal fronted by another tenant's registration or grouping another tenant's application — both contradict settled ownership decisions and would breach tenant isolation at the presentation layer. Two violations added, plus the agreed stewardship warning for same-tenant portals whose application sets diverge.

decisions.title: The enablement gate had forgotten offerings
decisions.reasoning: The no-parity decision requires enablement to check subscriptions AND offerings covering the enablement scope, but only the subscription half had been implemented — so an application could be enabled in a scope where its required capability is offered nowhere. Added as a separate shape with its own message and test rather than widening the existing gate, so each half fails distinguishably.

decisions.title: Grant derivation corrected; tenant onboarding named as a gap
decisions.reasoning: The seed channel grant derived from a database subscription — structurally valid, semantically nonsense. Channel grants now derive from the party registration. This exposed a real absence: platform- and tenant-dimension grants have no natural source because tenant onboarding is not modelled at all. Recorded as a named backlog gap, and the likely home for future tenant-level CAEP events.

decisions.title: Journey-definition governance made falsifiable
decisions.reasoning: The claim that journey-definition changes 'flow through the declaration machinery' was unfalsifiable prose: declarations could only declare the state of data planes, with no link to a journey definition. Added a JourneyDefinitionChange subclass of DesiredStateDeclaration mirroring ApplicationEnablement, so scope, rigor and supersession apply for real.

decisions.title: Sessions are per user per device; channel comes from device class
decisions.reasoning:
The platform issues one session per user per device, and concurrent session limits are configured per device class. Neither fact was expressible: there was no device concept at all, so the session identity rule could not be stated and the limits could not be checked.

Modelling the device also settles a question left open twice. Channel evidence was first assumed to come from the token's authorized party, which turned out to be wrong once the OAuth client_id proved to be only a protocol identifier. The real source is the device: the session manager knows whether it authenticated a browser or a mobile app, so for interactive sessions the delivery channel follows from the device class. Channel is a property of the session, not evidence carried in a token — which also explains why the api and agent channels have no device, since there is no interactive client to classify.

Two invariants: a principal holds at most one active session per device, and a principal's active sessions in a device class must not exceed the tenant's configured limit — a counting constraint that joins through tenant membership to find the applicable policy.
rejected: Merging device class into the delivery-channel vocabulary: they overlap for browser and mobile but differ in extension, since api and agent are channels with no device — one vocabulary would have members that cannot be devices.
Deriving channel from the OAuth client registration: the client_id is a protocol identifier for the session manager's registration, one per audience, carrying no channel information at all.

Modelling concurrent-session policy as a governed declaration: left as plain configuration for now and recorded as an open question, since it is a security control with no approver — the same asymmetry route bindings had before D43.

decisions.title: Tenant membership connects the principal to the tenant
decisions.reasoning:
Asking why there is no Identity class exposed a hole. Three senses of 'identity' already had homes — the authenticable entity is Principal, a name in a namespace is split between the firm-canonical identifier and the issuer-scoped SubjectIdentifier, and the assertion at a moment is an authentication event. But a fourth sense, persona or capacity, had none: no property anywhere linked a Principal to a Tenant.

The consequence was severe. Routes resolve the tenant, tokens resolve the principal, and every entitlement grant is held by a tenant — so nothing verified that this principal may act for that tenant at all. As written, a valid token for any principal presented at any tenant's address satisfied every modelled check.

Modelled as TenantMembership: a first-class, approved, lifecycle-bearing record following the Subscription pattern rather than a bare property, because 'when did this principal gain access to this tenant and who approved it' is the access-review question. One principal may hold memberships in several tenants — consultants and dual-capacity staff are ordinary. Capacity is recorded but grants nothing by itself; what a capacity means inside an application is Level-3.

The keystone invariant is on admission: no admission decision may evaluate a tenant's grants for a principal holding no active membership in that tenant. Two supporting invariants require human approval for activation, mirroring subscriptions, and forbid two active memberships for one principal in one tenant, which would leave it ambiguous which membership authorised a request.
rejected: A plain mayActForTenant property: closes the reachability hole but records no lifecycle — no approver, no date, nothing an access review can read.

A Persona class that entitlement grants are held by, replacing tenant-held grants: more expressive and handles dual capacity natively, but it reopens the settled grant model, and a tenant's subscriptions genuinely are tenant-level — that was never the missing fact.
An Identity class as a synonym for Principal: two words for one concept.

An Identity class merging the canonical identifier with issuer-scoped subjects: re-conflates exactly what the subject-identifier work separated, since one says what we call a principal and the other resolves an unknown subject to one.

decisions.title: Sessions are sender-constrained, DPoP-style
decisions.reasoning:
A session cookie is a bearer artifact: steal the handle, replay it, you are in. Adopting DPoP (RFC 9449) with the confirmation binding of RFC 7800 changes that, and it changes what the handle IS. The handle identifies the session; the proof-of-possession key authenticates the presenter. A stolen handle without the private key grants nothing, so the cookie stops being credential-like and becomes an identifier — which is why ProofOfPossessionKey is modelled as its own class rather than a Credential subclass: it is generated by the presenter rather than issued by an identity provider, and it proves continuity of possession rather than an identity claim.

Four invariants follow, and the third is the one that matters most in practice: a session must be bound to a key at all; a handle must resolve to exactly one session; a sender-constrained session must not issue tokens that are unbound or bound to a different key — constraint laundering, where the session is protected but the tokens it hands out are not; and one key must not confirm sessions belonging to different principals.

Deliberately not modelled: the per-request DPoP proof itself, with its htm, htu, jti and ath claims. Proofs are per-request and transient, and the same reasoning that keeps per-request capability usage out of the graph applies here — what is durable and governable is the key binding, not the evidence of any single request.
rejected: Modelling the proof-of-possession key as a Credential subclass: a credential is issued by an identity provider and proves an identity claim, while this key is presenter-generated and proves possession — merging them would make issuedBy meaningless for half the instances.
Modelling the per-request DPoP proof as a first-class node: per-request volume with no competency question behind it; replay prevention via jti is an enforcement concern, not a governance one.

decisions.title: Route-to-tenant binding is governed desired state
decisions.reasoning:
Ingress resolves tenant context from domain and path, bound to a tenant in ingress route configuration — not from any token claim. That binding is therefore the root of tenant.access: changing it changes who a request is treated as. But it was distributed configuration with no declaration, no approver and no supersession history, while every write into a capability data plane required all three. That asymmetry was not deliberate, and it put the most tenant-sensitive control outside the governance pipeline.

Modelled by adding hostname, pathPrefix and boundToTenant to the ingress route, and a RouteBindingChange subclass of DesiredStateDeclaration — the third use of that pattern after application enablement and journey-definition changes — so route bindings inherit scope, approval rigor and supersession for free. Three invariants follow: one address must resolve to exactly one tenant; a tenant-bound route must state the hostname it resolves from; and a tenant binding must have an approved declaration behind it. The control-plane module now imports ingress, which states the governance relationship honestly rather than leaving it implicit.
rejected: Modelling route matching without governing it: describes reality but leaves tenant resolution as the one security-critical control with no approver, which is the asymmetry that prompted the work.
Leaving the binding unmodelled and treating it as infrastructure detail: tenant.access cannot be explained, let alone audited, without the binding that resolves the tenant.

decisions.title: Events are PROV activities
decisions.reasoning: core:PlatformEvent is a subclass of prov:Activity, so authentication, decision, mutation and change events inherit lineage tooling for free — and causal chaining between events (prov:wasInformedBy) is available at zero modelling cost when credential and session state-change events land.

decisions.title: Decision point and enforcement point are disjoint
decisions.reasoning: P13 requires that the component rendering a decision differs from the one acting on it, and the vocabulary already had both roles — but nothing forbade one individual carrying both types, so a fused decide-and-enforce component passed every shape. Closed with an OWL disjointness axiom in core and a SHACL shape on the decision point, with a negative instance so the invariant demonstrably fires (P10). Core moves to 0.5.0.
rejected: Leaving separation as a review-time test: the fitness criterion is 'enforced or enforceable', and this one was cheap to enforce.
A shape on the enforcement point instead: equivalent; the decision point is the side the principle names first.

decisions.title: The index build fails on a dangling reference
decisions.reasoning: Principles, decisions, shapes, terms and explainer steps reference one another by name, and the build resolved those references but only warned when one was missing — so a principle claiming a shape that did not exist passed CI. Under P15 a lost input must not silently lower assurance: the build now records every unresolved reference, prints it as a failure, writes no index and exits non-zero. Demonstrated to fire at promotion by injecting a bogus shape name.
rejected: Keeping the warning and adding a separate lint step: two places to look, and CI already runs the build.
Writing the index anyway and failing afterwards: a half-correct index in the working tree invites committing it.

decisions.title: The isolation model is enforced; blast radius is a formal question
decisions.reasoning: D08 recorded that one data-driven constraint enforces whatever isolation model a capability declares, but no shape referenced the property: the model was declared, instantiated once, and enforced nowhere — a hope, not a control (P10), and a recorded enforcement that did not exist (P15). IsolationModelShape rejects a data plane serving more than one tenant under a cell-per-tenant capability, with a negative instance so it fires. The backlog question 'which tenants' data planes are reachable from a declaration' is the principle's testability clause made concrete; it is promoted to CQ-8 with a query CI runs, answering reach as scope containment exactly as D04 defines it.
rejected: A shape per isolation model value: D08's point was one constraint whatever the capability claims; 'shared' needs no constraint, so one shape covers the closed set.
Amending D08 to drop the enforcement claim: the claim was the right design, only undelivered.

decisions.title: Executor and requesting principal are mandatory
decisions.reasoning: P17's test — can the graph walk from this record to the responsible principal with no optional hop — failed on the two most security-relevant records. A policy change required its changed policy and a human approval but not its executor, so CQ-3 ('who executed each change') would return nothing for it; a decision required its policy, action, outcome and decision point but not its requesting principal, and the membership check silently passed a decision with no subject because its pattern only matches when one is present. Both properties become mandatory with a typed principal; the positive corpus already carried them on every instance, and two negative instances make the invariants fire.
rejected: Requiring performedBy on every platform event instead: observations (capability use) are evidence rather than actions and carry no actor by design; the actor property differs per event type, so the requirement belongs on each shape.

Leaving the executor optional because a workload may execute under automation: automation still runs as a workload principal (P14), and an unnamed one is exactly what the sole-writer invariant exists to catch.

principles.title: The boundary, not the resource
principles.statement: Coarse-grained platform authorization protects the right to enter an application and deployment boundary; resource authorization protects the right to perform an operation on an application resource. The platform never learns what is inside an application.
principles.test: Could the platform still evaluate this check if every application were replaced by an opaque identifier with no documentation? If not, it is not a platform entitlement.
principles.consequences: One enforcement stack serves many independently developed applications only because the vocabulary ingress evaluates stays small, closed and platform-owned. Application verbs cannot enter the action scheme; application entitlements cannot enter the dimension scheme; a business object is never resolved above the boundary.
principles.fitness: generative (6 decisions, 2 invariants) · testable (the opacity question) · enforced

principles.title: Governance defines; enforcement actuates
principles.statement: Whatever defines desired state or entitlement never actuates or enforces it, and whatever enforces never defines. The control plane defines and ingress enforces; the management plane declares and capability control planes write; offerings are intent and data planes are actuation.
principles.test: Which component defines this, and which executes it? If the answer is the same component, the design is wrong.
principles.consequences: Every data-plane write traces to a declaration; every entitlement grant traces to the governance object it was projected from; route bindings are declarations rather than loose configuration; the management plane holds no write path into a data plane.

principles.title: Agents execute; humans authorize
principles.statement: Automation may act, but a human must be accountable for every grant of authority: policy changes, declarations in rigor-requiring scopes, subscription activations, membership admissions and requirement confirmations all carry a human approval. Revocation is the deliberate exception — taking access away fast is safe; giving it back is the boundary.
principles.test: Does this change grant authority? Then which human is accountable for it?
principles.consequences: Approvals by workload principals alone never satisfy an invariant. The same asymmetry recurs wherever authority is conferred, and its planned counterpart is that revocation needs no approval while reinstatement does.

principles.title: The token is evidence; the grant is authority
principles.statement: A token proves who is calling and in what context; it never carries what they may do. Authority is a grant the control plane projects to the enforcement point, revocable without re-minting anything. Claims freeze at issuance; grants do not.
principles.test: Would this decision change if the token were re-minted? If yes, authority has leaked into evidence.
principles.consequences: Entitlements are never minted into tokens; scope and permissions claims are ignored at ingress; the OAuth client_id is a protocol identifier and never a basis for a decision; sender-constraining makes a stolen token useless rather than merely short-lived.

principles.title: An identifier resolves to an entity; it does not substitute for one
principles.statement: A domain resolves to a tenant, a subject value to a principal, a handle to a session, a client_id to a registration. Each is evidence that resolves to an entity the model holds separately, with its own lifecycle and relationships. Collapsing the two loses everything the entity carries beyond that one resolution path.
principles.test: Is this thing the entity, or a way of finding it? If it is a way of finding it, model the entity and the resolution separately.
principles.consequences: Tenants are first-class rather than route bindings; subject identifiers are reified rather than strings on principals; session handles resolve to sessions rather than being sessions; a device is nameable rather than only classified.

principles.title: OWL for semantics, SHACL for contracts
principles.statement: OWL defines meaning and licenses inference; SHACL is the data contract. rdfs:domain and rdfs:range are kept off shared properties, because under OWL semantics a domain axiom does not reject bad data — it infers a wrong type. Typing and cardinality live in shapes, where a breach is a report. sh:Violation rejects at ingestion; sh:Warning admits but routes to stewardship.
principles.test: Should a breach of this be rejected, or inferred around? If rejected, it is a shape, not an axiom.
principles.consequences: Every typed relationship in the model is stated in a shape, which is why the relationship graph is derived from SHACL rather than OWL. Cross-module typing needs no cross-module import.
principles.fitness: generative (every shape) · testable · enforced structurally — no shared property carries a domain or range

principles.title: Vocabularies are closed schemes of individuals
principles.statement: States, levels, outcomes, methods, dimensions, actions, channels, device classes and identifier formats are SKOS individuals in closed schemes, never subclasses. Individuals keep generic queries simple, make extension a data change rather than a hierarchy change, and — decisively — make closure checkable: 'is this term in the platform-owned scheme' is a one-line constraint.
principles.test: Is this a fixed set of governed values? Then a scheme of individuals, extended by a MINOR bump — not a class hierarchy.
principles.consequences: Nine schemes. Assurance levels additionally carry an integer rank so SHACL-SPARQL can compare them in order.
principles.fitness: generative (9 schemes, 5 decisions) · testable · enforced by scheme-membership checks

principles.title: Specifications, never products
principles.statement: The ontology aligns to public specifications and names no products. XACML's roles, OAuth and OIDC claims, NIST SP 800-63 levels, RFC 9493 subject identifiers, DPoP, AuthZEN's tuple and SPIFFE identity stay; a gateway API, an IdP vendor or a ticketing product does not. A vocabulary that encodes today's implementation ages badly and misleads readers into taking an implementation detail for a modelling commitment.
principles.test: Is this a public specification, or a vendor's product? Specifications may be named; products may not.
principles.consequences: Ingress terms describe the entry model itself; product names in definitions and seed data were removed; SPIFFE stays because it is a specification and the recorded identifier strategy.
principles.fitness: generative (applies to every term) · testable · review-time

principles.title: Questions before terms
principles.statement: A term exists to answer a competency question. Add the question first; a term with no question behind it is scope creep. Promotion to stable additionally requires a shape, positive and negative instances, and a recorded rationale.
principles.test: Which competency question does this term answer? If none, do not add it.
principles.consequences: Every modelling pass in this ontology began by writing the questions into the backlog. The build warns about terms with no recorded rationale so the gap is visible rather than silent.

principles.title: An invariant that cannot demonstrably fire does not count
principles.statement: Every violation-level constraint has a deliberately broken instance in the negative corpus, and CI asserts that it fires. A constraint that has never been seen to reject anything is a hope, not a control.
principles.test: Which negative-test instance trips this constraint, and does CI assert that it does?
principles.consequences: The negative corpus grows with every invariant; CI gate three names each expected violation by a fragment of its own message; the count of firing invariants is a reported metric.

principles.title: Every kind of statement has exactly one home
principles.statement: A definition denotes; rationale lives in decisions; enforcement in the shape's message; principles here; open questions in the competency backlog; examples in skos:example; history in the module description. Anything stated in two places drifts into two versions — and this layer exists because 'the token is evidence' had been restated in five.
principles.test: Where is the one home for this statement? Put it there, and reference it everywhere else.
principles.consequences: Definitions were cut to their denotation; the browser renders each home beside the others so duplication is visible; this file is the home for principles.
principles.fitness: generative (the definition-style pass, this layer) · testable · build-checked for references

principles.title: One path, no bypass
principles.statement: Every governed target — an application boundary, a data plane, an entitlement, a route binding — is reached through exactly one governed path. Anything arriving outside it is a violation, never an exception.
principles.test: Name the one governed path to this target. Can the proposal reach it any other way? Then either the invariant that rejects that way exists, or the proposal is not admissible.
principles.consequences: Every route is mediated by exactly one policy enforcement point before its upstream; a data plane has exactly one designated writer and a mutation with no declaration behind it is an orphan write; a grant without a derivation link is forbidden; a route binding with no declaration behind it is configured out of band; one address resolves to exactly one tenant. Bypass-class constraints carry violation severity, never warning: a bypass is rejected, not queued for stewardship. Where the bypass leaves no trace in the graph — an undeclared route — the rule is enforced as 'every declared path is mediated' and 'there is no undeclared path' stays a deployment assertion.
principles.fitness: generative (4 decisions, 6 invariants across request, write, authority and configuration paths) · testable · enforced — request-path instance enforced on declared paths only

principles.title: Decisions are policy-based and externalized
principles.statement: Every authorization decision evaluates a named policy and is rendered by a named decision point. The enforcement point that acts on it is a different component. No platform decision lives in the code that enforces it.
principles.test: Which policy does this decision evaluate, which decision point renders it, and which enforcement point acts on it? If any answer is 'the code', or two answers are the same component, the design is wrong.
principles.consequences: Every decision references the policy it evaluated, names exactly one decision point and has exactly one outcome; a permit below the policy's required assurance level is a violation; every route is mediated by exactly one enforcement point; a decision point is never also an enforcement point. The distributed entitlement configuration is itself a policy, so admission decisions satisfy the same shape as every other decision. Scope: platform decisions are the only decisions in the graph — for application decisions the rule is an architectural expectation, not an invariant, because P1 keeps application internals out of the graph.
principles.fitness: generative (3 decisions, 5 invariants) · testable · enforced — the decision/enforcement separation became enforceable only at promotion (D52)

principles.title: Principals are modelled uniformly
principles.statement: Humans, services and agents share one identity and authorization model. They differ by attributes and by permitted flows, never by separate mechanisms.
principles.test: Does this proposal add a class, property or shape that exists for one kind of principal only? Then is it a subtype, an attribute, or a permitted flow on the common model — or a second mechanism? Only the last is rejected.
principles.consequences: One Principal class with disjoint human and workload subclasses; every binding in authentication, sessions, membership and decisions types to the common class, so a mechanism that excluded a kind would need a new class to exist at all. Identifiers are naming facts under one property whatever their format — directory identifier or SPIFFE ID; credentials span passwords, FIDO2 registrations, client certificates and workload SVIDs; identity providers span the enterprise directory and the workload issuer. Kind-specific behaviour lives only in flows: approvals require a human principal (P3), a capability control plane's acting identity is a workload, devices exist only on interactive channels. Scope: agents are workloads until delegation enters the model — the agent-channel terms are deferred and 'under what delegation was this authority exercised' is a backlog question; machine-to-machine sessions are out of scope, so workload flows are modelled thinly beyond the acting-identity pattern.
principles.fitness: generative (2 decisions on uniformity, 4 on permitted flows) · testable · enforced structurally — the common class is the only binding target

principles.title: Trust boundaries fail closed
principles.statement: When a security decision cannot be made — because evidence is absent or stale, or the outcome is indeterminate — the request is denied. Loss of an input or component never silently lowers assurance: it is a rejection or a visible failure, never a warning that lets the request through.
principles.test: If this input is absent or stale, or the decision is indeterminate, what happens? If the answer is 'the request proceeds' or 'a warning', the design is wrong.
principles.consequences: Missing evidence is a violation, not a warning: an attribute without an authoritative issuer cannot be used in a decision; a decision names its decision point or is unattributable; admission without grants is admission without authority; a permit below the policy's required assurance level is rejected; a session with no proof-of-possession key, or a token bound to a different key or none, is rejected — sender constraining must not be lost at issuance; an active session must originate from a successful authentication. The method layer fails closed too: CI fails on a positive violation, a negative corpus that conforms, or an invariant that does not fire, and the index build fails on any dangling reference between principles, decisions, shapes, terms and explainers (D53). Known exception: a grant with no distribution timestamp is a warning, so a grant whose freshness cannot be shown is still enforceable; the open question 'how stale may a distributed grant be before ingress fails closed' must be answered — probably per dimension — before that severity is raised. Scope: the data contract and CI fail closed; the runtime half — what the enforcement point does on an Indeterminate or NotApplicable outcome — is not expressible in the graph, which records decisions and evidence, not behaviour in their absence.
principles.fitness: generative (7 invariants embody it; 2 decisions) · testable — found the fail-open build and the staleness warning on first application · enforced on the data contract and in CI; runtime denial is asserted

principles.title: Isolation boundaries are explicit and enforced
principles.statement: Every isolation boundary is stated in the model, and every crossing of it is rejected by an invariant. Tenant, administrative scope and a capability's isolation model are enforced today; environment and region are stated as scope facets pending their own invariants; zone is not modelled. The reach of any one declaration is bounded by scope containment.
principles.test: Which boundary does this cross, and which invariant rejects the crossing? A boundary with no rejecting invariant is a label, not a boundary.
principles.consequences: Tenant: a route serves only its bound tenant's applications, one address resolves to one tenant, admission requires membership, a grant confers exactly one tenant, a portal groups only its owner's applications. Scope: a declaration is bound to exactly one scope, a mutation's data plane must lie inside its declaration's scope (locality, D04), enablement and deployment outside offered scope are violations, and a control plane may not administer the scope holding its own declarations. Isolation model: a data plane under a cell-per-tenant capability serves at most one tenant (D54). Blast radius: the data planes reachable from a declaration are exactly those its scope contains — CQ-8 answers it, and the sole-writer and self-governance invariants bound who can act on them. Not yet enforced: environment and region are facets on scope nodes, to be promoted to closed schemes with rejecting invariants before stable; zone does not exist in the model. Runtime enforcement is asserted; the graph enforces the data contract and CI.
principles.fitness: generative (9 decisions, 14 invariants) · testable — found D08's undelivered invariant on first application · enforced for tenant, scope and isolation model; environment and region stated only

principles.title: Every action is traceable
principles.statement: Every request and every security-relevant state change leaves evidence that traces, hop by hop, to the responsible principal — the one who acted and, where P3 applies, the one who authorized. A record whose actor is optional is not evidence.
principles.test: For this record, who is the responsible principal, and can the graph walk from the record to them with no optional hop? If any hop is optional, the trace is a hope.
principles.consequences: Every platform event is a PROV activity with exactly one timestamp. Authentication events and journey executions name their principal; approvals name their approver; sessions name their principal and the execution that established them; a token inherits its session's confirmation; a grant carries its derivation; a decision names its decision point, policy, action and — from D55 — its requesting principal; a policy change names its executor and its human approver; a mutation with no executor fails the sole-writer constraint. Four formal questions are traces: CQ-3 who executed and approved each change, CQ-4 which source issued each attribute, CQ-5 the full assurance chain behind each permit, CQ-6 which changes each workload executed. Observation records (capability use) are evidence, not actions, and carry no actor by design. Known exception: sessions, credentials, memberships and subscriptions have state schemes but no state-transition events, so revocation, expiry and suspension leave no record in the graph — the credential-lifecycle and CAEP backlog, too large for a promotion. Observability in the metrics-and-logging sense is outside this model; traceability is the half it holds.
principles.fitness: generative (9 decisions, 12 invariants, 4 formal questions) · testable — found the optional executor on policy changes and the optional subject on decisions on first application · enforced on the data contract; state-transition events are the known gap

evaluatedNotPrinciples.why: One alignment axiom, applied once. It does not generate further decisions and offers no test to apply to a proposal. It is a well-chosen decision and stays one.
A specific vocabulary split. What is generative in it is the rule it applies — an identifier resolves to an entity and does not substitute for one — which is P5. The split itself is one decision.

evaluatedNotPrinciples.candidate: D49 — Decisions name the deciding PDP; XACML is the settled vocabulary
evaluatedNotPrinciples.why: Two specific choices: one required property, one vocabulary selection. The vocabulary half is an application of 'specifications, never products'. Neither half constrains future choices beyond itself.
A fact about the platform — capabilities are not everywhere — rather than a rule of design. Its modelling (offerings as intent, data planes as actuation) applies P2.
A topology choice with a stated condition for reversal. Generative only through P2, which it applies.

evaluatedNotPrinciples.candidate: Definition style: a definition denotes, nothing else
evaluatedNotPrinciples.why: Testable and generative, but a prose-quality rule rather than a design principle on its own. Its underlying rule — one home per kind of statement — is the principle, and it covers this and more.

The grant model implies allow-by-entitlement, and the Microsoft comparison surfaced the contrast, but it has never been decided. Recording it as a principle would be inventing one. Left as a question for the architecture group. Distinct from P15 (fail closed): P15 is the absence-of-decision rule — evidence missing or outcome indeterminate — not the absence-of-grant rule. Whether the absence of any grant is itself a deny remains this open question.

evaluatedNotPrinciples.candidate: Controls are enforced by platform, not delegated to applications
evaluatedNotPrinciples.verdict: not promoted — a corollary of P1 and P2; its one novel clause is unenforceable by construction
evaluatedNotPrinciples.why: Unqualified, 'controls' includes resource authorization, which P1 assigns to the application and which the platform never evaluates; the statement only holds once narrowed to platform controls (tenant resolution, session and token binding, platform entitlements, application admission). At that scope it is not generative: every decision it would claim is already attributed — route serves application (D48) and decisions name their PDP (D49) to P1, ingress as the enforcement point to P2, sender-constrained sessions to P4. Its residual clause, that applications do not re-enforce platform controls, has produced no decision and no shape, and cannot: P1 states the platform never learns what is inside an application, so no shape or gate can observe an application re-checking tenant or session. As worded it also fails testability in the wrong direction — 'is this control enforced by the platform?' answers yes for resource authorization, steering proposals toward the platform doing more. 'Delegated' additionally collides with P3, where delegation is a transfer of authority between agents. What survives is a consequence of P1, not a principle: a request that reaches an application has already passed every platform control, so the application neither re-enforces them nor is relied upon to.

evaluatedNotPrinciples.candidate: Capabilities are consumed through published contracts; consumers depend on contracts, not implementations; contracts are versioned and managed through a published change process
evaluatedNotPrinciples.verdict: not promoted — out of scope for this ontology; revisit pending a scoping decision
evaluatedNotPrinciples.why: Sound for the platform's interface-governance domain, but nothing in the identity-and-access ontology depends on it. Not generative: no decision or shape follows from it, and the ontology has no contract, version, interface or consumer term. Not testable in practice: 'which contract does this consumer depend on?' would be answered 'not applicable' by every proposal that enters this ontology. Not enforceable: nothing could enforce it until Contract and ContractVersion terms exist, and under P9 those cannot be added before a competency question asks for them — none does. The first sentence already has an identity-domain counterpart that is enforced: a subscription targets a capability and never a data plane, and enablement references the capability (D11, P2 — offerings are intent, data planes are actuation). Versioning and a published change process have no counterpart. Not to be conflated with the ontology's own governance (semantic versioning, deprecation, change control), which applies this rule to the ontology as an artefact, not to platform capabilities.
evaluatedNotPrinciples.todo: Scoping decision pending: does contract versioning enter this ontology, or a separate service-catalogue ontology this one links to (recommended)? If it enters, the route is P9 — competency questions first (which contract version does this application depend on at this deployment scope; which consumers are affected by deprecating a contract version), then Contract and ContractVersion terms, then shapes.

evaluatedNotPrinciples.candidate: Substitutability is designed in at the dependency seams that matter; for critical dependencies such as DNS, CDN and edge services the platform supports active substitution rather than only migration
evaluatedNotPrinciples.verdict: not promoted — out of scope for this ontology; a resilience principle for the platform's infrastructure
evaluatedNotPrinciples.why: Not generative: no decision or shape follows from it; DNS and CDN do not exist in the model, and the edge — routes, enforcement points, upstream services — carries nothing about substitution or alternate providers. Not testable in practice: 'can this dependency be substituted while active?' cannot be asked of the graph, which has no infrastructure-dependency concept; the one dependency property, hard dependency between capabilities, is about provisioning order. Not enforceable until 'critical dependency' and 'substitute' become terms, which P9 blocks until a competency question asks for them. What the model already says about seams: the intent/actuation split (P2) and subscriptions targeting a capability rather than a data plane (D11) let a realization be swapped without touching a consumer, and a route forwards to at least one upstream, so several may stand behind one — substitution is structurally permitted at those seams, neither required nor forbidden. The seam that matters in this domain is the identity provider, and there the model shows substitution designed out by the standard: a subject identifier is scoped to exactly one issuer (RFC 9493, D30), so substituting the identity provider re-keys every principal's naming fact — a migration with re-issuance, never an active substitution.
evaluatedNotPrinciples.todo: Scoping decision pending: substitutability of infrastructure dependencies belongs to a platform-engineering or resilience ontology this one could link to. The one in-scope piece is recorded as a backlog question under Subject identifiers: which principals' subject identifiers are bound to a given issuer, and what would re-issuance under another require?

explainers.title: What is evaluated where
explainers.subtitle: Platform entitlements at ingress, application authorization inside the boundary
explainers.summary: Coarse-grained platform authorization protects the right to enter an application and deployment boundary; resource authorization protects the right to perform an operation on an application resource. This walkthrough covers where that line sits, what sits on each side, and how the model stops the line from moving quietly.

steps.heading: The three layers
steps.body:
Coarse-grained platform authorization protects the right to enter an application and deployment boundary. Resource authorization protects the right to perform an operation on an application resource. Everything below follows from holding those two apart.

The symmetry is exact and worth reading twice: both are authorization, both have a subject, both end in a decision. What differs is the object being protected — a boundary in one case, a resource in the other — and that difference is what makes one platform-owned and the other application-owned. A boundary is the platform's to define because the platform put it there; a resource belongs to whoever built the application behind it.

One enforcement stack serves many independently developed applications, and that only works if the vocabulary ingress evaluates stays small and stable, and if nothing application-specific can enter it. The control plane defines entitlements; ingress enforces them; applications own everything past the boundary.

steps.heading: A request, resolved
steps.body:
Take a concrete request:

POST https://api.company.com/digital-bank/transactions/12345

Before any entitlement is evaluated, ingress resolves it to a platform endpoint. The route registry matches the domain and path, and everything the platform needs falls out of governed configuration — none of it asserted by the caller.

What ingress then knows is that a request is attempting to enter the digital bank's transactions boundary, in prod, in us-west-2. What it does not know, and never needs to, is that /12345 identifies an order. That is the line: the endpoint is registered platform configuration, the object behind it is application data.

With that resolved, the authorization request is the XACML tuple — subject Alice, action ACCESS, resource the application access endpoint — with the tenant, environment, region, channel, session and assurance as context. The decision point answers one question: may Alice, acting for this tenant, cross this boundary. Permit or Deny.

rows: the session and its journey execution
the token's sub, via a subject identifier

steps.heading: One request, three checkpoints
steps.body:
The three layers become three checkpoints on a single request, and the first distinction to make is between the first two — because it is the one people collapse.

Ingress is the enforcement point. It resolves and it enforces, but it does not decide: the domain and path give it the tenant, the application and the endpoint; the token gives it the principal; the cookie handle with its proof gives it the session; the journey definition gives it the channel and the assurance. None of that is a decision. It is the context a decision needs.

The platform PDP decides one thing — may this request cross into the application boundary — and answers Permit or Deny. Every check it makes is answerable with the application as an opaque identifier: membership, the five dimensions, enablement in scope, coverage, assurance. Nothing about what the application does.

Past the boundary, the application PDP decides what the subject may do, and the ontology does not model it. That is a decision rather than an omission, and it is enforced: an application verb cannot enter the platform action scheme, and an entitlement outside the platform dimensions cannot be evaluated at ingress. The request path ends at /12345, which is an order — the platform never learns that, and must not.

rows: Route bindings, subject identifier, session handle, journey definition — resolution only
Membership, the five dimensions, enablement scope, subscription and offering coverage, assurance
Roles, business rules, record-level access, limits — application-owned, out of scope
